hints: Count every carbon, hydrogen and oxygen in Fig. 5.1 carefully, remembering that each corner of the ring and each line end is a carbon with enough hydrogens to make four bonds.
walkthrough:
Count atoms to get the molecular formula**
Look closely at Fig. 5.1 with me. The ring plus side chain gives 6 carbons, 8 hydrogens and 6 oxygens in total, so the molecular formula is $\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{8}\text{O}_{6}$. Remember skeletal lines hide carbons and hydrogens, so count the two $\text{OH}$ groups on the ring, the $\text{CH(OH)CH}_{2}\text{OH}$ side chain, the ring $\text{C-O}$ and the ester $\text{C=O}$.

Simplify to the empirical formula**
Empirical means simplest whole number ratio. All the subscripts 6, 8, 6 share a common factor of 2. Divide through by 2 to get $\text{C}_{3}\text{H}_{4}\text{O}_{3}$.

hints: Recall the titration link $n = c \times V$ and convert the titre volume from $\text{cm}^{3}$ to $\text{dm}^{3}$ by dividing by 1000 before multiplying.
walkthrough:
Set up the moles equation**
For any solution, amount links to concentration and volume by $$n = c \times V$$ Here $c = 5.00 \times 10^{-3} \text{ mol dm}^{-3}$ for $\text{I}_{2}(\text{aq})$.

Convert volume and substitute**
The titre is $36.65 \text{ cm}^{3} = 36.65/1000 = 0.03665 \text{ dm}^{3}$. So $$n(\text{I}_{2}) = 5.00 \times 10^{-3} \times 0.03665 = 1.8325 \times 10^{-4} \text{ mol}$$ which rounds to $1.83 \times 10^{-4} \text{ mol}$.

hints: Use Fig. 5.2 to find the reacting ratio of $\text{I}_{2}$ to vitamin C, then use $m = n \times M_{r}$ with $M_{r} = 176$ to get the mass in the $25.0 \text{ cm}^{3}$ sample and scale up to $100.0 \text{ cm}^{3}$.
Recall percentage by mass is (mass of vitamin C / 150.0) $\times$ 100, so divide your total mass by the lemon mass.
walkthrough:
Link moles of iodine to moles of vitamin C**
Look at Fig. 5.2. One $\text{I}_{2}$ reacts with one vitamin C molecule to give M, so the ratio is 1:1. That means $$n(\text{vitamin C in }25.0 \text{ cm}^{3}) = n(\text{I}_{2}) = 1.8325 \times 10^{-4} \text{ mol}$$

Convert to mass and scale to the whole lemon extract**
Use $$m = n \times M_{r}$$ with $M_{r} = 176$: $$m = 1.8325 \times 10^{-4} \times 176 = 0.03225 \text{ g in }25.0 \text{ cm}^{3}$$ Solution L is $100.0 \text{ cm}^{3}$, which is 4 times the titrated sample, so $$m(\text{total}) = 0.03225 \times 4 = 0.129 \text{ g}$$ This is the mass from $150.0 \text{ g}$ of lemon.

Calculate percentage by mass**
Percentage means part per hundred of the lemon: $$\text{percentage} = \frac{m(\text{vitamin C})}{150.0} \times 100 = \frac{0.129}{150.0} \times 100 = 0.086\%$$ Values $0.086\%$ to $0.087\%$ are accepted due to rounding.

Final answer: mass in $25.0 \text{ cm}^{3} = 1.8325 \times 10^{-4} \times 176 = 0.03225 \text{ g}$; mass in $100.0 \text{ cm}^{3} = 0.03225 \times 4 = 0.129 \text{ g}$; percentage $= (0.129/150.0) \times 100 = 0.086\%$

hints: Compare the two structures in Fig. 5.2 bond by bond and use Table 5.2 to decide which bonds responsible for each wavenumber range are lost and which remain in M.
walkthrough:
Check what the 1500-1680 range means**
From Table 5.2, $1500-1680 \text{ cm}^{-1}$ is $\text{C=C}$ of an alkene. Vitamin C has a $\text{C=C}$ in the five membered ring, so it shows this band. In M that double bond is oxidised to two $\text{C=O}$ ketone groups, so no $\text{C=C}$ remains. Mark absent (x or blank) for M.

Check the C-H and O-H bands**
$2850-2950 \text{ cm}^{-1}$ is $\text{C-H}$ alkane stretch. Both vitamin C and M still contain the $\text{CH(OH)CH}_{2}\text{OH}$ side chain with $\text{C-H}$ bonds, so this band stays present (✓). $3200-3650 \text{ cm}^{-1}$ is $\text{O-H}$ hydroxy stretch. Vitamin C has four $\text{OH}$ groups, M still has the two side chain $\text{OH}$ groups, so hydroxy $\text{O-H}$ is still present (✓).
Final answer: $1500-1680 \text{ cm}^{-1}$: absent in M (x); $2850-2950 \text{ cm}^{-1}$: present in M (✓); $3200-3650 \text{ cm}^{-1}$: present in M (✓)
